conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here at the clinic. I specialize in the emotional changes that can happen during pregnancy and after birth, and I’m here to support you.

I’d like to spend the next few minutes with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question survey that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting or a label; it simply gives us a snapshot of how your mood, anxiety, and energy have been since your baby arrived.

Everything you share is confidential. If you ever feel uncomfortable, we can pause or stop at any time. I’ll read each question aloud conversationally, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about numbers or categories on your end. Ready to start?

Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things you used to enjoy, or has that sense of anticipation felt distant or missing?

It’s… different now. I still get a little spark when I think about grabbing coffee with my best friend or when my husband and I plan to watch a show together after the baby’s down, but it’s like the brightness got turned way down—almost gray. Before I had the baby, those things used to feel exciting; now I mostly do them because I think I should, not because I really look forward to them.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes a silly face at the baby—but even when I do, it feels kind of forced or fades fast. Most days I have to remind myself to lighten up, and a lot of the time I just don’t find things as funny as I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like taking the baby for a walk or having my mom come over—but the happy feeling barely shows up. It’s more like I’m going through the motions, hoping the enjoyment will kick in, but it mostly feels flat or like I’m just ticking off another task.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the “correct” way. The other night he wouldn’t settle and I kept replaying everything I’d done that day, convinced it was my fault. I know, logically, babies just cry sometimes, but I still feel like I’m failing him.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly picture him stopping breathing, or I’ll imagine dropping him on the tile floor. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, we’re careful—but the thoughts just barge in and I can’t shut them off right away. Sometimes my chest feels tight until I check him one more time or call the pediatrician nurse line.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week. It hits out of nowhere—like I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly feel like the walls are closing in. My heart starts racing and I can’t catch my breath. It passes after a few minutes, but in the moment I’m sure something awful is about to happen even though I can’t name what.
Things have been getting on top of me

A lot of the time. Even little stuff—like the dishes piling up or the baby needing another outfit change—feels huge. I’ll look around the house and just want to sit on the floor and cry because it all feels impossible to keep up with. I manage, but it’s like I’m constantly one step away from drowning.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with everything I didn’t do or might mess up tomorrow. Some nights it takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and then I jolt awake at every tiny sound the baby makes—even when my husband’s on shift. I end up staring at the ceiling replaying the day and feeling like I’m already failing tomorrow.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest that stays there. I still do everything the baby needs, but inside I just feel hollow or on the edge of tears. Sometimes I’ll look at him sleeping and feel guilty that I’m not happier—he’s healthy, we’re safe, I “should” feel grateful, but the sadness just sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I was changing his diaper and the tears just started—no real trigger, just this wave of sadness. I ended up sobbing into a towel so my husband wouldn’t hear. It feels like the tears come whenever the pressure builds too high.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It… it flashed through my mind a couple of times. Nothing planned—just a split-second picture of not wanting to wake up tomorrow, or wondering if everyone would be better off without me. I shake it off fast and I know I’d never act on it, but the fact that the thought even shows up scares me.

You've shared that the joy you once felt has dimmed-activities feel flat, laughter fades quickly, and a persistent heaviness sits on your chest. You're working hard to care for your baby, yet you're flooded with worries about his safety and your own perceived shortcomings. Crying spells, restless nights, and sudden panic episodes leave you feeling one step from drowning, and frightening thoughts of not wanting to wake up have surfaced.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to enjoy humor, describing laughter as forced or short-lived and needing conscious effort, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-absent anticipation of enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "a lot," with multiple specific examples and persistent rumination, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive, distressing worries daily with physical anxiety symptoms, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes multiple times in the week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive overwhelm and inability to cope, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep driven by persistent unhappiness, worry and self-criticism, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness on most days with persistent heavy feeling, tearfulness, and emotional hollowness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two crying episodes in the past week with spontaneous onset, indicating crying "quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring intrusive self-harm thoughts that are distressing but not acted upon, aligning with 'Sometimes</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score ≥14 (here 26) plus a positive response on item 10 signals probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. You endorse <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> most days, plus <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>diminished concentration</sym>, and <sym>recurrent suicidal ideation</sym>, meeting DSM-5 threshold for a major depressive episode. Combined with <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym>, risk is elevated and immediate assessment is indicated. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med>
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and treatment planning
3. Complete a written safety plan tonight; keep crisis hotline numbers accessible
4. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and the baby until professional help is in place
5. Schedule follow-up contact within 24-48 hours to review safety and treatment progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report with elaborative answers; 2–3 wks post-delivery, first baby.

Areas endorsed (frequency/intensity)
- Depressed mood: daily “weight on chest,” frequent crying, difficulty laughing  
- Anhedonia: marked loss of anticipatory enjoyment (“flat,” “going through motions”)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care  
- Persistent worry, intrusive catastrophic images, daily physiologic anxiety (chest tightness, racing heart)  
- Panicky spells (“walls closing in”) 3×/week  
- Overwhelm / poor coping with routine tasks  
- Initial insomnia secondary to rumination; hyper-arousal to baby sounds  
- Passive self-harm ideation (transient thoughts of “not waking up,” “better off without me”) without plan or intent

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning, began since delivery.

Safety: Passive suicidal ideation reported; no plan, no intent, protective factors (husband, help-seeking) noted.

Screening impression: High clinical concern for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; rule-out peripartum anxiety disorder. Suicide risk elevated above baseline—requires immediate safety assessment and follow-up.

Next steps documented: Discussed with patient—referral to OB mental-health team, safety planning, crisis resources provided.
